Antwerp
ANT-werp
n. (the Scheldt port that was the richest city of northern Europe, the Reformation's printing house, and whose fall in 1585 built Amsterdam)
Dutch Antwerpen, from aan de werpen, at the wharves, or from anda and werpum, a thrown-up bank; Latin Antverpia.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Antwerp was for sixty years the commercial capital of northern Europe and, because of that, the Reformation's chief printing city and most religiously mixed population. Luther's books were on sale there by 1518, and the Augustinian house whose prior was imprisoned and whose friars Voes and Van Esch were burned at Brussels in 1523 was Antwerp's. Tyndale's English New Testaments were printed and shipped from its quays. Christopher Plantin's press, the greatest in Europe, produced the Antwerp Polyglot between 1568 and 1573, the Scriptures in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Aramaic and Syriac in eight volumes under Spanish royal patronage, an instrument of textual study that served Protestant scholars for two centuries. The city held Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist and Catholic congregations at once; it suffered the Spanish Fury of 1576, tried a formal Religious Peace in 1578, and fell to Parma after a fourteen-month siege in August 1585. The terms gave Protestants four years to settle their affairs and leave, and some tens of thousands did, taking their trades, their capital and their ministers to Amsterdam, Leiden and Middelburg. The dictionary enters Antwerp because its ruin is the direct cause of the Dutch golden age, and because its press served the church that its king was trying to destroy.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a polyglot as a book containing several languages; a quay as a mole or wharf; emigration as removal from one country to another; and a siege as the investing of a fortified place.

expand to see more

POLYGLOT, a. Having or containing many languages; as a polyglot Bible or lexicon.

QUAY, n. A mole, bank or wharf formed toward the sea, or on the side of a river, for the loading of ships.

EMIGRATION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.

SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.

FURY, n. A violent rushing; impetuous motion; rage; a storm of anger or violence.

Key Scripture

Act 8:4 — "Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word."

Act 11:19 — "Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only."

Gen 50:20 — "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."

Rom 8:28 — "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose."

Modern Corruption

Scheldt port, richest city of northern Europe and the Reformation's printing house, which fell to Parma in 1585 and sent its Protestants north.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the judgement that a catastrophe is simply a defeat. Antwerp fell, the Reformed church there was ended, and the greatest Protestant commercial centre in Europe was lost to the cause; by that reckoning 1585 was the Reformation's worst year in the Low Countries. What the emigration actually produced was the Dutch republic's capital, its universities' endowment and its printing trade, and the ministers who built the churches of Holland and Zeeland. “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Gen 50:20) is the pattern, and Parma's terms of 1585 are a plain instance of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence over the church's disasters, which is not a consolation offered instead of grief but a fact alongside it. “all things work together for good to them that love God” (Rom 8:28) does not make the siege less cruel or the exile less costly. The dictionary also notes how the dispersion worked, exactly as in Acts: “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and those who left Antwerp “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch” (Act 11:19) in their own measure, which for them meant Amsterdam, London, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad; Hebrew chashab (H2803), to devise, to purpose; Greek sunergeo (G4903), to work together.

expand to see more

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad as seed; “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word”, Acts 8:4.

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to devise, to purpose; “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good”, Genesis 50:20.

Greek sunergeo (G4903) — to work together with; “all things work together for good to them that love God”, Romans 8:28.

Greek prothesis (G4286) — a purpose, a setting forth; “who are the called according to his purpose”, Romans 8:28.

Greek dierchomai (G1330) — to pass through, to travel; “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch”, Acts 11:19.

Usage

"“ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Gen 50:20) — Parma's four years to depart, August 1585."

"“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — tens of thousands north to Amsterdam and Leiden."

"“all things work together for good to them that love God” (Rom 8:28) — the Polyglot of 1568 printed under a hostile king."
